new_statements.quote: Sauf ces dérogations à la règle générale, qui s'expliquent d'ailleurs par la phonétique, la syllabe qui porte l'accent en latin la conserve en provençal comme dans les autres langues romanes. (pp. 42-43) [...] Les noms propres d'origine étrangère ont souvent l'accent sur la dernière syllabe, principalement les noms terminés en -us : Eumenidús, Dedalús, Tantalús, Jesús ; Semiramís, Florís, Biblís ; Eneàs ; Cesàr ; Camillà, Sibillà. (p. 43) [...] La plupart de ces mots sont, comme en ancien français, des proparoxytons apparents et des formes savantes ; ils sont rares en poésie et làgrema ou pólvera, par exemple, y comptent pour deux syllabes [...] Nous considérons donc tous ces mots comme paroxytons. (p. 128)
new_statements.translation: Apart from these departures from the general rule, which are in any case explained by phonetics, the syllable that bears the accent in Latin keeps it in Provençal, as in the other Romance languages. [...] Proper names of foreign origin often have the accent on the last syllable, chiefly names ending in -us: Eumenidús, Dedalús, Tantalús, Jesús; Semiramís, Florís, Biblís; Eneàs; Cesàr; Camillà, Sibillà. [...] Most of these words are, as in Old French, apparent proparoxytones and learned forms; they are rare in poetry and làgrema or pólvera, for example, count there as two syllables [...] We therefore treat all these words as paroxytones.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for Old Provençal has an EMPTY rule, so this supplies one rather than agreeing or contradicting: stress on the Latin-stressed syllable, restricted to final or penult. Describes the medieval literary language ('ancien provençal').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress stays on the syllable that bore the Latin accent (after the Vulgar Latin shifts: parietem > parét, filiolum > filhòl, integrum > entier, recomposition renéga, viderunt > víron, infinitives cazér, sabér). In practice words are oxytone or paroxytone; Latin proparoxytones lost the penult and the remaining 'apparent proparoxytones' (làgrema, pólvera) are learned forms that scan as two syllables, i.e. paroxytones. Place-names in -anum show a later Provençal shift (Romà > Roma).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated in the Accentuation section (the phonology chapter uses 'partie posttonique' / pretonic terminology only).
new_statements.exceptions: Foreign proper names and learned Greek/Latin words often stressed on the final syllable per the Leys d'Amors (Jesús, Cesàr, acirologiá, paragogé); words in -ica stressed on i (gramatíca); troubadours occasionally shift stress at the rhyme (Alexandrés : bes); Celtic place-names kept initial stress (Némausus > Nemze); Provençal shift in -anum place-names.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the medieval literary language of the troubadours (ancien provençal / Altprovenzalisch = Old Occitan), the same variety Paden 1998 covers; Appel and Anglade draw the two-position statement from the 14th-century Toulouse Leys d'Amors (accen agut = final, accen lonc = penult), and Appel notes the Old Gospel of John fragment and Boethius as the only manuscripts marking stress.

new_statements.quote: § 20. Der Exspirationsdruck liegt im Provenzalischen auf der letzten (accen agut) oder der vorletzten (accen lonc; rimas longas „weibliche Reime") Silbe des Wortes. Dies sind die beiden einzigen Tonlagen, welche die Leys (I 88) anerkennen. Wir werden bei der Besprechung der tonlosen Vokale sehen (§ 41), daß auch die Existenz von Proparoxytonis zuzugeben ist: mónegue, mónega, pórtegue, pértega, mánegue, lágrema, pólvera, sénebe, sénede, cóvede [...] (p. 24) § 21. Der Ton liegt im Provenzalischen auf der Silbe, welche der lateinischen betonten entspricht. (p. 25) [scanned 'acccn Jone; rimas Tongas' read as 'accen lonc; rimas longas']
new_statements.translation: § 20. In Provençal the expiratory stress lies on the last (accen agut) or the penultimate (accen lonc; rimas longas 'feminine rhymes') syllable of the word. These are the only two stress positions that the Leys [d'Amors] (I 88) recognize. We shall see in the discussion of the unstressed vowels (§ 41) that the existence of proparoxytones must also be admitted: mónegue, mónega, pórtegue, pértega, mánegue, lágrema, pólvera, sénebe, sénede, cóvede [...] § 21. In Provençal the stress lies on the syllable corresponding to the Latin stressed one.

Describes the troubadour language, citing the 14th-c. Leys d'Amors.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is final (accen agut) or penultimate (accen lonc) — the only two positions the Leys d'Amors recognize — with a handful of proparoxytones admitted (mónegue, lágrema, pólvera). Position is inherited from Latin (§21). Distribution: oxytones may end in any vowel/diphthong or (voiceless) consonant; paroxytones end in the vowels a and e (plus i/o in loans and dialect forms) or the consonants s (inflection: fólhas, cantas), r, n (coser, creisser, amen, joven), l (avol, angel). Scribes do not mark stress except in the Old Gospel of John fragment and Boethius.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §35-36 (pp. 39-40) treat the word-initial syllable preceding the main stress as 'nebentonig' (secondary-stressed): àpòderár, recelar; §40b 'Zwei Silben zwischen Neben- und Hauptton' (p. 46).
new_statements.exceptions: A few proparoxytones (mónegue, lágrema, pólvera, sénebe, cóvede); sentence-stress loss in pronouns/adverbs/prepositions (ama'l filh, deves > daus); Latin words and consonant-final foreign names pronounced as oxytones (dominús, París, Semiramís, Eneás, Cesár, esperít); vowel-final ones vacillate (Cavillá, Sibillá, Jericó vs Pári, Eléna, Séneca, gramática); rhyme licences (jóves with -és); princeps stressed variously.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the medieval literary language of the troubadours (ancien provençal / Altprovenzalisch = Old Occitan), the same variety Paden 1998 covers; Appel and Anglade draw the two-position statement from the 14th-century Toulouse Leys d'Amors (accen agut = final, accen lonc = penult), and Appel notes the Old Gospel of John fragment and Boethius as the only manuscripts marking stress.

new_statements.quote: 15. In volkstümlichen Wörtern, d. h. Wörtern, welche lautgesetzliche Entwicklung erfuhren, bleibt der Platz des lateinischen Akzentes fast ausnahmslos bewahrt. Von den lateinischen Proparoxytonis verlegen zwei Gruppen schon im Vulgärlateinischen ihren Akzent auf die vorletzte Silbe, einmal die auf -iolum, -eolum, -ierem ausgehenden Wörter und dann die Wörter, deren letzte Silbe mit Muta + r auslautete (p. 13) [...] 18. Lateinische Wortformen nehmen den Akzent auf die letzte Silbe, z. B. Dominí, ebenso fremde Eigennamen, die kein lebendes Sprachgut waren, z. B. Biblís, Dedalús, aber Eléna. — Bisweilen erlauben sich die Trobadors, den Akzent dem Reime zulieb zu verändern, z. B. preián (3. Pl. Präs.): dan. (p. 15)
new_statements.translation: 15. In popular words, i.e. words that underwent regular sound-law development, the place of the Latin accent is preserved almost without exception. Of the Latin proparoxytones, two groups already moved their accent to the penultimate syllable in Vulgar Latin: the words ending in -iolum, -eolum, -ierem, and the words whose last syllable began with stop + r [...] 18. Latin word-forms take the accent on the last syllable, e.g. Dominí, likewise foreign proper names that were not living vocabulary, e.g. Biblís, Dedalús, but Eléna. — Occasionally the troubadours permit themselves to change the accent for the sake of the rhyme, e.g. preián (3 pl. pres.) : dan.

new_statements.quote: In general, Occitan words ending in a consonant are stressed on the final syllable: [...] Words ending in a vowel are stressed on the penult, or next-to-final syllable [...] The position of stress in Occitan almost always corresponds to the CL etymon or its reflexes in other Romance languages (cf. ch. 11). A syllable may, however, be inherently stressed or unstressed in defiance of this generalization. [...] Un- stressed final syllables ending in consonants occur in words in -er such as nominative singular mélher ‘wife’ and sénher ‘lord,’ [...] Such stresses are indicated in the headwords of the Glossary.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Grandgent 1905 secs. 16-17: accent stays on the Vulgar Latin syllable, i.e. lexically inherited) and as the three read statements (Anglade 1921 pp. 42-43; Appel 1918 sec. 20: final or penultimate syllable, with some proparoxytones; Schultz-Gora 1906 sec. 15): Paden states that OOc stress position 'almost always corresponds to the CL etymon'. Adds (refines): the synchronic default by final segment (consonant-final -> final stress, vowel-final -> penultimate), lexical exceptions in both directions marked in the Glossary headwords (aisi, enaisi, Jaufre oxytone despite final vowel; melher, senher, planher, avol, joven paroxytone despite final consonant; n-mobile…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Occitan word stress continues the Latin accent position (lexically inherited): as a surface default, words ending in a consonant are oxytone (cantar, partir, cantatz) and words ending in a vowel are paroxytone (canta, domna, paire, glazi); lexical exceptions both ways exist and are marked in the glossary (aisi, Jaufre with stressed final vowel; melher, senher, planher, avol, joven with unstressed final closed syllable); declensional -s does not move the stress; in verbs the morphology fixes it (cantas, cantan, venguen unstressed final; cantara, mori stressed final); proparoxytones are marginal (Tripol, learned calici) because the Latin unstressed penult fell (DOMINAM > domna).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No synchronic statement on secondary stress in OOc; only the diachronic remark p. 112 (file line 2186) 'Classical Latin vowels in initial syllables carried secondary stress' and p. ~205 (line 4006) on proclitic DOMINE > en losing independent stress.
new_statements.exceptions: inherently stressed final vowels: aisi, enaisi, aquo (scanned 'ac@'), Jaufre; n-mobile words stressed finally whether or not -n is written (certan/certa); unstressed consonant-final syllables: nom. sg. melher, senher, inf. planher (unstressed -er class, also conoiser type), avol, joven; declensional -s (domnas, paires) no shift; shifting declension senher/senhor, molher (VL hiatus shift MULIEREM > molher); verb endings; triphthongs stressed on the middle element; proparoxytones Tripol, calici and other learned -i nouns; foreign proper names not discussed here (Anglade's Jesus-type oxytones not mentioned in this section).
new_statements.identity_note: Old Provençal = Old Occitan (the medieval literary koine of the troubadours, 11th-14th c.); Paden 1998 uses the name Old Occitan for the same language.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on the page image we hold (p. 12, sec. 17) and in the scanned text we hold (secs. 16-19, pp. 11-13). (2) Deciding source is a 1905 historical grammar; for an extinct medieval language that is the appropriate genre, and three independent historical grammars downloaded now (Schultz-Gora 1906 sec. 15, Appel 1918 sec. 21 p. 25, Anglade 1921 pp. 42-43, the last being Glottolog's listed grammar) state the identical rule: Old Provençal stress sits on the syllable that bore the Latin accent, with listed lexical exceptions (learned words, foreign names oxytone, analogical verb shifts, rhyme licences). That supports the lexical coding (position etymologically given; both oxytones and paroxytones occur with the same final shapes, e.g. sénher vs molhér). (3) Only real gap is Paden 1998, the modern 610-pp reference, not open; unlikely to overturn the classification. (4) Status adequate; action
